title: 5 Freshmen Democratic Lawmakers to Watch

5 Freshmen Democratic Lawmakers to Watch

Meet the potential foreign-policy and national security big hitters of the next Congress.

By Rachel Oswald, a staff writer at Foreign Policy.

A large group of people stand on the steps of the U.S. Capitol.

Newly elected members of the U.S. House of Representatives pose for a photo on the steps of the U.S. Capitol in Washington on Nov. 12. Jim Watson/AFP via Getty Images

November 17, 2026, 3:31 PM

In January, dozens of new Democratic lawmakers will enter the House of Representatives—many with strong U.S. foreign-policy and national security views.

Analysis and arguments.

And while they won’t have the seniority to chair major committees, they could still prove incredibly influential. Just look at the lawmakers who swept in during the last Democratic wave election in 2018 and went on to become household names—figures such as Ilhan Omar, Rashida Tlaib, and Deb Haaland. Some have gone on to win governorships and Senate seats. One—Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez—is even widely speculated to be considering a high-profile run at the 2028 Democratic presidential nomination.

Analysis and arguments.

And while they won’t have the seniority to chair major committees, they could still prove incredibly influential. Just look at the lawmakers who swept in during the last Democratic wave election in 2018 and went on to become household names—figures such as Ilhan Omar, Rashida Tlaib, and Deb Haaland. Some have gone on to win governorships and Senate seats. One—Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez—is even widely speculated to be considering a high-profile run at the 2028 Democratic presidential nomination.
Here are five incoming House Democrats who could end up being just as formidable presences in the next Congress, especially on foreign policy and national security.

Fred Wellman
Retired Army Lt. Col. Fred Wellman rode the blue tsunami to topple a longtime Republican lawmaker. His background as a helicopter pilot with multiple combat tours followed by work in political communications and veterans’ advocacy could position him to be a thorn in the side of the Trump administration and Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth.
Wellman served for 22 years in the Army and saw combat four times, including during the first Gulf War and three tours in Iraq. Formerly a lifelong Republican, Wellman switched parties after becoming disgusted with Donald Trump’s disparagement of former Sen. John McCain’s prisoner-of-war status. He would go on to be a veterans’ affairs advisor and later the executive director of the Lincoln Project, a political action committee that drew national attention in the 2020 presidential contest for its acerbic ads that lampooned Trump’s character and record.
Wellman has been a fierce critic of Trump’s decision to launch a war against Iran without congressional authorization. He supports continued military assistance to Ukraine and the Block the Bombs Act, legislation popular with progressives that would prohibit the export of some of the United States’ most powerful bombs to Israel.

Eileen Laubacher
Eileen Laubacher, a retired Navy rear admiral, is another former Republican who flipped a deeply red district. Laubacher narrowly unseated one of MAGA’s most prominent and polarizing House members, Rep. Lauren Boebert, in Colorado’s reddest district.
Laubacher’s distinguished 34-year Navy career, which focused on intelligence matters and South Asia, could propel her to assignments on Capitol Hill’s national security committees, such as House Armed Services or House Intelligence, where her insider knowledge of U.S. surveillance technology and the defense-industrial base bureaucracy is likely to be valued.
In her final years of military service, Laubacher served as defense attaché to India and then on the National Security Council during the Biden administration as the point person for South Asia. During her stint as the top defense official at the U.S. Embassy in New Delhi, Laubacher was credited with playing an important role in facilitating U.S. support for the Indian military during a series of violent 2020 standoffs with the Chinese army along the two countries’ disputed Himalayan border.
Her campaign focused on affordability issues and connecting Trump’s tariff policies and the Iran war to higher cost of living, as well as improving care and services for veterans. She is a member of the Blue Dogs, a caucus of moderate and conservative-leaning House Democrats. Laubacher wants an end to U.S. taxpayer-financed military support for Israel but supports the transfer of weapons to the country on a “case by case basis.”

Melat Kiros
Also hailing from Colorado but from the opposite wing of the Democratic Party is Melat Kiros, a democratic socialist who at 29 years old will become the youngest female lawmaker in Congress in January. Kiros immigrated as a baby with her family from Ethiopia.
As a junior corporate attorney, she was fired from her job at a prominent law firm for refusing to take down an open letter she published defending law students who expressed pro-Palestinian views in the weeks after Hamas’s Oct. 7, 2023, attack on Israel. Kiros, who has accused Israel of committing genocide, drew connections to her family’s own experiences, having lost family members to what she called the recent “genocidal war against Tigrayans by the Ethiopian and Eritrean governments.”
This summer, Kiros successfully challenged from the left the 15-term incumbent progressive lawmaker Rep. Diana DeGette to win the Democratic nomination for the solid blue Denver-area congressional seat. She argued that DeGette and other establishment Democrats had been ineffective in combating Trump. During the primary, Kiros made Israel a distinguishing issue between herself and DeGette. She supports an arms embargo to the country that would cover even defensive systems such as the Iron Dome missile shield.
In the House, Kiros is expected to align with other far-left young progressives such as Ocasio-Cortez. Although Kiros received critical primary campaign backing from the Democratic Socialists of America, she has said she does not share the national organization’s position that the United States should withdraw from NATO.

Brad Lander
Like Kiros, Brad Lander successfully ran to the left of an establishment Democrat in a deep blue district where support for Israel was a key dividing issue. But Lander’s Jewish faith and victory over a pro-Israel incumbent in one of the most Jewish districts in the United States (New York’s 10th) could make him a potent Capitol Hill foil for the Israeli government.
Lander, a former New York City councilman and comptroller, is a political ally of New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani. And he has already been mixing it up online and offline with members of both Israel’s political opposition and Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s far-right government. Like many other progressive House Democrats, Lander, whose district includes Lower Manhattan and Brooklyn, supports the Block the Bombs Act.
When former Israeli Prime Minister Yair Lapid wrote on X shortly after the U.S. midterm elections that his country’s next government should prioritize repairing ties with moderate Democrats in Congress as well as embark on a public relations tour of the United States, Lander pushed back hard.
“[Y]ou’re not listening to what American voters—Jewish and non-Jewish—are saying,” Lander wrote on X in response. “We aren’t starving for a barnstorming tour. We’re hungry to see respect for international law and human rights.”
Just a few weeks earlier during a solidarity visit to the West Bank to help Palestinian farmers harvest their olive crop, Lander was detained for several hours by the Israeli military, which said it was because his trip presented a “security risk.”
“Yet one more element of escalating, and very clearly state-sponsored ethnic cleansing,” Lander wrote of the experience.

Nancy Lacore
Speaking of potent foils, Hegseth may face one of his own making when he is eventually called to testify before the House oversight committees.
Nancy Lacore is another retired Navy admiral who narrowly flipped a solidly conservative district in the midterms. But Lacore, who won her South Carolina House seat by just over 3,000 votes, is also one of the highest-ranking officers to be ousted by Hegseth. Her 35-year Navy career, including her most recent position as the chief of the Navy Reserve, would seem to make her a strong candidate for membership on the House Armed Services Committee.
Lacore has said she doesn’t know why Hegseth fired her, but she went on to make her opposition to his leadership a central tenet of her campaign. “Pete Hegseth is the most unqualified secretary that this nation has seen,” Lacore said in an interview with CBS News after winning election. “He has caused significant damage to us as a country and put us at risk and really damaged the readiness of our entire military force.”
The retired three-star vice admiral was a registered Republican until 2016, when Trump became the party’s leader. In January, she will become the highest-ranking female military officer ever to serve in Congress.
